title: Before the Bell
passages:
Sára woke before light, as she always did, and listened. Under the floorboards the iron wheel in the wall clicked over one tooth, the way it did every night, though no hand had ever turned it. On the kitchen table sat two things with paper tags. There had never been two.

Ákos was dressed, his letter in his pocket — the printing works at Vaskapu, answer due today. "Say something," he said. "Say I can go." "Not before the work," said Sára. "Say something about me." "Ask me after the Point," she said.

The first tag read: *For the woman in the Toll House. Open before the bell.* Every tag they had ever read said where a thing went. This one said open. The second thing was a doll, jointed, its face scraped smooth, tagged *For the house on the Point, before the bell, or it goes back.* Nobody had lived on the Point since the fire the year Ákos was born.

"You don't open them," Ákos said. "That's the rule. The Halászys opened theirs and forgot each other's names, and they've been polite about it ever since, and theirs was their own knocker back after forty years, so don't tell me nobody sends these." Sára tore the packet open. The tag had said to. Inside, a scrap of paper, and on it a name: VERA. She knew it the way you know a song you haven't heard in years. Ákos wrote VERA in his notebook over the first line, and did not read her what he crossed out. He put his letter back in his pocket, unopened. "Low tide's at noon." They took the lantern and the good boots and went out onto the causeway while the water still let them.

The water had pulled off the causeway stones and left them streaming weed. Ákos went first with the unlit lantern, counting the gaps under his breath the way he counted everything, and Sára came behind with the doll wrapped in her shawl, carrying it the way you carry something that is not yours.

At the Point the road gave out in a yard of ash and nettles. The house had no roof and no floor. The chimney stood, and the burnt beams lay across the rooms where they had fallen. Behind it a smokehouse still had a door, and a woman came out of it with an armful of sticks. She was seventy or more, in a man's coat, and she looked at Sára for a long time.

"Vera," she said.

Ákos wrote it in the notebook, standing in the wet ash. "You know her."

"I know what she was called." The woman set down her sticks. "Ilka Dálnoky. I keep the yard. Seventeen years I've kept it, and you're the fourth to come up this road with one of those." She nodded at the shawl. "Shelf is inside. Don't put it in yet."

On a plank shelf in the smokehouse stood three dolls with their faces scraped smooth, side by side, and the remains of a fourth swept into a corner. Ilka gave the rule the way she might give the weather. The doll goes in the back room, on the hearthstone, and you are off the Point before the bell. "It has a face by evening," she said. "Whose, I've never stayed to see."

Sára went into the back room alone and knelt and set the doll on the hearthstone, which was small, the size a child could lie across. When she stood up something had gone out of her. She looked at Ákos and said, "You have your mother's chin." Then she stopped. "I had her face this morning. I had it on the causeway."

Ákos wrote that down too. "That's three." He put the notebook in his coat and took out the letter, the answer due today, and held it a moment before putting it away again. "I'm going to Vaskapu on the evening tide. The work's done here. You can lose the rest without me."
